title: Structured output, and why JSON mode changed what was buildable
story:
Ask for a particular output format in the instructions and you will get it, most of the time. That phrase is doing all the damage. A parser that fails one call in fifty is not a small defect — it is a permanent branch in every consumer, a retry path, a fallback, a log nobody reads, and eventually a person on a rota. The cost of unreliable structure is not the failures, it is the machinery built to survive them.

Which is why the fix was not a better instruction. It was a change to how the text is produced at all.

Generation chooses one token at a time from a distribution over the vocabulary. Nothing requires you to leave that distribution alone. If you know which tokens could possibly come next without breaking the structure you demanded, you can drive the probability of every other token to zero before the choice is made. The model does not have to cooperate, because the tokens that would violate the structure are not on offer.

Willard and Louf set out an efficient way to do this. They reformulate generation as transitions between the states of a finite-state machine, which lets you construct an index over the vocabulary mapping each state to the tokens that are valid continuations from it. At sampling time the disallowed tokens are masked before a token is chosen, with no rescanning of the sequence, and with a hash map for the index the step costs a constant on average — the index being built outside the sampling procedure entirely. The result is model agnostic, enforces the constraints you supply, and guarantees the structure of the generated text while adding little overhead.

Read that last sentence as a change in category rather than a performance improvement. Before, the output was prose that a program hoped to parse. After, the output is a value another program can consume without hoping. The lightweight text-based syntax for interchanging structured data — the format specified by RFC 8259, which everything in this part of the field speaks — stops being a formatting preference and becomes an interface.

That is what changed what was buildable. A model whose output parses by construction can be a component: its result can be the arguments to a function, a row to be written, a decision that routes a request, a step in a plan another part of the system will execute. Everything now discussed as tool use, function calling, or agents rests on this, and none of it was reasonable when the output was prose with a format request attached.

Now the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that will bite you.

Valid is not correct. A guarantee about structure is a guarantee about shape and nothing else. Every field will be present and every type will match, and the values inside can be entirely wrong. Worse, the guarantee cuts the other way in one specific respect: a structure that must be completed will be completed. A required field gets filled whether or not the information exists, and constraining the decoder removes parse failures while quietly increasing the pressure to invent, because there is no longer any way for the output to trail off, hedge, or decline.

The design response follows directly, and it is the thing to remember from this lesson. Give the structure somewhere to put nothing. A field for not found, an option for not applicable, a variant of the response that means the evidence did not support an answer. If the only shapes your schema admits are shapes that assert something, you have not removed fabrication from your system — you have made it mandatory and then guaranteed that it parses.

And after parsing, check the content, because nothing so far has. Do the referenced identifiers exist. Is the number inside the range this field can actually take. Does the chosen option make sense given the request. Treat the structured output the way you would treat a well-formed request from a client you do not control: the shape being right is where validation begins, not where it ends.

problem.name: Guaranteeing the shape of generated output
problem.shape: Another program has to consume what the model produces, and the model produces text.
tell: consumers have grown retry paths and fallbacks for output that sometimes fails to parse
the format is requested in the instructions and nothing enforces it
the schema has no way to express that the answer is unknown or absent
the output parses and nobody checks whether the values are possible
problem.move: Constrain the decoder so invalid tokens are masked before sampling and the structure holds by construction, then give the schema a way to express nothing, and validate the values after parsing as you would any untrusted request.
problem.invariant: Masking the tokens that would break the structure makes a valid parse independent of the model's cooperation, so parse failure stops being a failure mode at all.
problem.breaks: The guarantee covers shape and not content, and a structure that must be completed will be completed — so enforcing a schema with no empty option converts a missing answer into an invented one.

cost.time: the mask is applied at each step, which adds little overhead when the index is built ahead of sampling
cost.space: the index over the vocabulary has to be constructed and held, which is memory spent outside the request
cost.beats: requesting a format in the instructions, which works most of the time and pushes the cost into every consumer, and parsing prose after the fact, which fails on exactly the awkward cases

worked.problem: What is the difference between asking for a format and enforcing one, and what does enforcement not give you?
worked.reasoning:
Asking is a request that will be honoured most of the time. Enforcing changes what can be produced at all.

The cost of most of the time is what makes the distinction matter. A parse failure once in fifty calls means every consumer grows a branch for it — a retry, a fallback, a log, eventually somebody on a rota. The machinery built to survive unreliable structure costs more than the failures do.

Enforcement works at the point of generation. Text is produced one token at a time from a distribution over the vocabulary, and nothing obliges you to leave that distribution alone. If you know which tokens could come next without breaking the required structure, you can mask every other token before the choice is made. Cooperation stops being necessary, because the violating tokens are not on offer.

The efficient form of this comes from Willard and Louf, who reformulate generation as transitions between the states of a finite-state machine and construct an index over the vocabulary mapping each state to its valid continuations. Disallowed tokens are masked before sampling with no rescanning, a hash map makes the step cost constant on average, and the index is built outside the sampling procedure. It is model agnostic, guarantees the structure of the generated text, and adds little overhead.

What that buys is a change in category: the output goes from prose a program hopes to parse to a value a program consumes. That is what makes function arguments, routing decisions and tool calls reasonable to build on at all.

What enforcement does not give me is correctness. Every field present and every type matching says nothing about the values. And there is a sharper edge: a structure that must be completed will be completed, so a required field gets filled whether or not the information exists. Constraining the decoder removes parse failures while increasing the pressure to invent, because the output can no longer hedge or trail off.

So I give the schema somewhere to put nothing — a not-found value, a not-applicable option, a response variant meaning the evidence did not support an answer. Without that I have not removed fabrication, I have made it mandatory and guaranteed that it parses.

And I validate the content after parsing: do the referenced identifiers exist, is the number in the range this field can really take, does the option make sense for the request. Well-formed is where validation starts.

problem.practice: Take a schema your system uses and ask it a question whose answer is genuinely not in the material. Watch a complete, well-typed, entirely invented object come back. Then add an explicit variant meaning the answer was not available and ask again. That before and after is the whole lesson, and it takes ten minutes.

beats.broke: A format asked for in the instructions is honoured most of the time, and the exceptions force a retry path, a fallback and a human into every consumer.
beats.fix: Mask the tokens that would break the structure before each choice is made, so a valid parse is produced by construction rather than by cooperation.
beats.cost: Shape is guaranteed and content is not, and a required structure must be completed — so without an explicit empty option, enforcement makes invention mandatory.

interview.q: What is the difference between asking for a format and enforcing one, and what does enforcement not give you?
interview.trap: Treating a guaranteed parse as a guaranteed answer. Constrained decoding removes parse failures and increases the pressure to invent, because the output can no longer hedge or decline.
interview.answer:
Asking is a request honoured most of the time, and most of the time is what costs you: a failure once in fifty calls puts a retry path, a fallback and eventually a person into every consumer.

Enforcing works at generation time. Text is produced one token at a time from a distribution, and you can mask every token that would break the required structure before the choice is made, so cooperation is not needed. Willard and Louf give the efficient form: reformulate generation as transitions between the states of a finite-state machine, build an index over the vocabulary mapping each state to its valid continuations, mask disallowed tokens before sampling with no rescanning, and with a hash map the step costs a constant on average while the index is built outside sampling. It is model agnostic and guarantees the structure with little overhead.

That is a change in category rather than a speed-up: the output stops being prose a program hopes to parse and becomes a value a program consumes, which is what makes function arguments and tool calls buildable at all.

What it does not give me is correctness. Fields present and types matching say nothing about values. And it cuts the other way in one respect — a structure that must be completed will be completed, so a required field gets filled whether or not the information exists. Parse failures go away and the pressure to invent goes up.

So I give the schema somewhere to put nothing: a not-found value, a not-applicable option, a variant meaning the evidence did not support an answer. Otherwise fabrication is not removed, it is mandatory and guaranteed to parse. And after parsing I check the content — do the identifiers exist, is the number in a possible range — because a well-formed request from a client I do not control is where validation begins.
